discovery: The cavity method and statistical-physics theory of random constraint satisfaction and inference problems (survey propagation, clustering and phase transitions in computational hardness)
motivation: The nominees turned the theory of spin glasses into a predictive tool for problems far beyond magnetism. Mézard developed the cavity method, which gives the replica-symmetry-breaking solution a clear probabilistic meaning. With Zecchina he extended it to random constraint satisfaction problems such as K-SAT and colouring. Their 2002 work predicted a clustering (dynamical) transition and a satisfiability threshold, and it yielded survey propagation, an algorithm that solves instances far beyond earlier methods. Montanari and collaborators refined this picture of phase transitions in random structures and connected it rigorously to message-passing algorithms (approximate message passing) used in inference, compressed sensing and learning. Many of these predictions have since been proved by mathematicians. The work shows that ideas about hidden order in disorder give exact, testable predictions about computation and information. It now underpins the statistical physics of machine learning.
